name: Pacifism
info: Pacifism is the opposition to war or violence, ranging from the rejection of all warfare to the belief that disputes can be settled peacefully; it has ancient precedents, took organised form in the peace movements from 1815 and gained its name in 1901.

facts.thinkers: Desiderius Erasmus, one of the most outspoken pacifists of the Renaissance; William Penn, Quaker founder of Pennsylvania; Immanuel Kant, Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Jeremy Bentham, Enlightenment writers on peace; Leo Tolstoy, who revived interest in pacifism in his late works; Mahatma Gandhi, pioneer of satyagraha; Bertha von Suttner, the first woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize; Martin Luther King Jr., who used Gandhian nonviolent resistance
facts.texts: Desiderius Erasmus, The Praise of Folly (1509) and The Complaint of Peace (1517); Immanuel Kant, Thoughts on Perpetual Peace; Henry David Thoreau, Civil Disobedience; Leo Tolstoy, The Kingdom of God Is Within You; Bertha von Suttner, Die Waffen nieder! (1889); Simone Weil, The Iliad or the Poem of Force; Aldous Huxley, Ends and Means (1937)
facts.ideas: rejection of war as always wrong; peaceful resolution of international disputes; institutional pacifism, the abolition of the military; nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience; conscientious objection; ahimsa, to do no harm; anarcho-pacifism; pragmatic pacifism, which holds that the costs of war are so high that better ways of settling disputes must be found
facts.today: peace churches such as the Quakers, Mennonites and Church of the Brethren; Christian denominations and groups including the Catholic Worker Movement and Pax Christi; Buddhist, Jain and Hindu traditions of ahimsa; green parties that list nonviolence among their key values; constitutions that reject war, among them Italy's, Germany's and Japan's; Costa Rica, which has had no military since 1948

t: Pacifism covers a spectrum from the belief that international disputes can and should be settled peacefully to opposition to violence under any circumstance, even in defence of self and others.

Its organised form dates from 1815 and 1816, when the New York Peace Society and the London Peace Society were founded, and it drew on two strands of thought: the secular Enlightenment and the evangelical religious revival.

Mahatma Gandhi's satyagraha served as inspiration to Martin Luther King Jr. and many others in the civil rights movement, while critics from Hitler to Orwell to Jan Narveson attacked pacifism on very different grounds.
dyk: On 1 December 1948 President José Figueres Ferrer of Costa Rica abolished the Costa Rican military, and in 1949 the abolition was introduced in Article 12 of the constitution.
ev: The Quakers repudiate violence in all forms and adhere to a strictly pacifist interpretation of Christianity
The New York Peace Society is founded, and the London Peace Society follows in 1816
The London Peace Society convenes the first International Peace Congress in London
The word pacifism, coined by Émile Arnaud, is adopted at the tenth Universal Peace Congress in Glasgow
Dick Sheppard establishes the Peace Pledge Union, which totally renounces war and aggression
British activists form the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament with Bertrand Russell as its president

sections.origins:
Pacifism is the opposition to war or violence. The word was coined by the French peace campaigner Émile Arnaud and adopted by other peace activists at the tenth Universal Peace Congress in Glasgow in 1901. A related term is ahimsa, to do no harm, a core philosophy in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Modern connotations have been explicated since the 19th century, but ancient references abound.

During the Warring States period in China the Mohist School opposed aggressive war between the feudal states and used its defensive strategies to protect smaller states from larger ones, hoping to dissuade feudal lords from costly warfare. The Seven Military Classics view warfare negatively and as a last resort. In Ancient Greece pacifism seems not to have existed except as a broad moral guideline against violence between individuals. The play Lysistrata by Aristophanes is fictional and comical, and its message seems to stem from frustration with the Peloponnesian War rather than from a philosophical position, but Euripides expressed strong anti-war ideas in The Trojan Women. Roman writers including Propertius, Tibullus and Ovid rejected the militarism of Roman society, and Maximilian of Tebessa, a Christian conscientious objector, was killed for refusing to be conscripted.

Many have understood Jesus of Nazareth to have been a pacifist, drawing on the Sermon on the Mount and its injunctions to turn the other cheek and love one's enemies. Others deny it and cite his driving of traders from the temple and the passage in Luke 22:36 about buying a sword; pacifists have typically explained that verse as the fulfilment of prophecy.
sections.ideas:
Pacifism covers a spectrum of views. It includes the belief that international disputes can and should be resolved peacefully, calls for the abolition of the military and war (institutional pacifism), opposition to any organisation of society through governmental force (anarchist or libertarian pacifism), and opposition to violence under any circumstance, even defence of self and others. The historians Peter Brock and Thomas Paul Socknat define pacifism in the sense generally accepted in English-speaking areas as an unconditional rejection of all forms of warfare. The philosopher Jenny Teichman calls its main form anti-warism, and Brian Orend summarises her view: for the pacifist, war is always wrong.

Pacifism may rest on moral principle, a deontological view that some point along the spectrum from war to interpersonal violence becomes morally wrong, or on pragmatism, a consequentialist view that the costs of war are so substantial that better ways of resolving disputes must be found. Absolute pacifists hold that human life is so valuable that a human should never be killed and war never conducted, even in self-defence; conditional pacifism draws on just war theory and may allow defence.

Some pacifists follow nonviolence, believing that nonviolent action is morally superior or most effective, though some support physical force in emergency defence of self or others. Not all civil resistance rests on a rejection of all violence: many leaders of such movements were not absolute pacifists, and the marchers from Selma to Montgomery in 1965 called for armed protection.
sections.spread:
From the 16th century the Protestant Reformation gave rise to the historic peace churches, foremost among them the Quakers, Amish, Mennonites, Hutterites and Church of the Brethren. Desiderius Erasmus argued strongly against warfare in The Praise of Folly (1509) and The Complaint of Peace (1517). Pacifist ideals then coalesced at the end of the 18th century from two strands, the secular Enlightenment, represented by Rousseau, Kant and Jeremy Bentham, and the evangelical revival that had helped the campaign against slavery, represented by William Wilberforce.

The first peace movements appeared in 1815 and 1816: the New York Peace Society, founded by David Low Dodge, and the London Peace Society, founded by William Allen. The London society convened the first International Peace Congress in 1843, with Elihu Burritt and Henry Richard behind it, and the first continental congress met in Brussels in 1848. Randal Cremer and Frédéric Passy founded the Inter-Parliamentary Union in 1889. Leo Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God Is Within You inspired a movement named after Tolstoy and was a major early influence on Gandhi, and Bertha von Suttner's novel Die Waffen nieder! made her a leading figure.

After 1900 peace movements focused on arbitration treaties and the Hague conventions. Between the wars organisations such as the War Resisters' International, the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom and the Peace Pledge Union drew tens of thousands of Europeans. Gandhi led dozens of nonviolent campaigns between 1917 and 1947, and in 1957 and 1958 the Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy and the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament were formed against the nuclear arms race.
sections.power:
Pacifism was seldom the basis of a state. The Quaker William Penn, founder of the Province of Pennsylvania, employed an anti-militarist public policy, and the colony was essentially unarmed for the 75 years from 1681 to 1756 and experienced little or no warfare. Costa Rica abolished its military in 1948, and the budget once spent on it now goes to health care and education. Several constitutions reject war: Article 11 of the Italian Constitution repudiates war as an instrument offending the liberty of the peoples, and the German, French, Danish and Japanese constitutions of the 1940s and 1950s hold similar provisions.

Where pacifists held no power, states often acted against them. The United States passed the Sedition Act of 1918. Between the world wars pacifist literature and public advocacy were banned in Italy under Mussolini, Germany after Hitler's rise, Spain under Franco and the Soviet Union under Stalin, where pacifism was denounced as cowardice. In Nazi Germany pacifists were dealt with harshly: Carl von Ossietzky and Olaf Kullmann died after imprisonment in concentration camps, and the Austrian farmer Franz Jägerstätter was executed in 1943 for refusing to serve in the Wehrmacht.

The Moriori of the Chatham Islands practised pacifism by order of their ancestor Nunuku-whenua. In 1835 invading Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama Māori from Taranaki killed, enslaved and cannibalised them, and the Moriori were almost completely annihilated.
sections.critiques:
A common argument holds that violence may be used to prevent further violence. It rests on consequentialism: foreign troops ending a dictator's oppression may save millions of lives, even if many thousands die in the war. Pacifists on deontological grounds oppose such action, and others reply that nonviolence may not save lives at once but would in the long run. The argument from Axis aggression holds that, had Germany, Italy and Japan not been defeated militarily, many more people would have died under their rule. Some pacifists changed their position: Bertrand Russell called his stance on Nazism relative pacifism, and E. M. Forster and Leonard Woolf rejected their earlier pacifism.

George Orwell, in Notes on Nationalism (1945), characterised pacifism as a form of nationalism and wrote that most pacifists belonged to obscure religious sects or were humanitarians who preferred not to follow their thoughts further; he also claimed that a small group of pacifist intellectuals were moved by hatred of western democracy and admiration of totalitarianism. Hitler in his Second Book held that pacifism would disappear when war ceased to serve booty-hungry individuals or nations, and Hermann Göring said at Nuremberg that denouncing pacifists was part of the Nazi seizure of power.

Jan Narveson argued that absolute pacifism is self-contradictory because it creates a paradox of rights. Peter Gelderloos argued that pacifism serves the interests of the state. Anne Appelbaum argued that pacifism in response to the Russo-Ukrainian War overlooks the lessons of history. Others have proposed social defence, relying on civil resistance, developed by Adam Roberts and Gene Sharp, though no country has adopted it as the sole basis of its defence.
sections.legacy:
Pacifism took many forms within religions. The historic peace churches have always held that Jesus himself taught and practised pacifism, and Catholic figures such as Dorothy Day and Thomas Merton were committed pacifists, although the Roman Catholic Church officially maintains the legitimacy of just war. Ahimsa is central to Hinduism and Jainism, and Buddhist peace activists include Thích Nhất Hạnh and Nichidatsu Fujii. Most Muslims are not strict pacifists, but Khān Abdul Ghaffār Khān, a devout Muslim nicknamed the Frontier Gandhi, founded the nonviolent Khudai Khidmatgar movement in 1929. Judaism is not a pacifist religion, though it holds peace highly desirable.

Gandhi's satyagraha, the resistance of tyranny through civil disobedience that also sought to change the heart of the opponent, inspired civil rights movements worldwide. Martin Luther King Jr. used Gandhian methods against racial segregation in the United States, and the 1986 People Power Revolution in the Philippines is among later examples. At Parihaka in New Zealand, Te Whiti-o-Rongomai led nonviolent resistance to land confiscations that proved more successful than violent resistance.

Several European governments such as Switzerland, Greece, Norway and Germany offer civilian service to conscientious objectors. Green parties list nonviolence as one of their key values, though in power they often compromise: the German Greens in Gerhard Schröder's cabinet supported German troops in Afghanistan in 2001. Philosophers such as Robert L. Holmes have argued that waging war in the modern era is unjustifiable and that one can be a pragmatic pacifist.

summary: Pacifism is the opposition to war or violence, from the belief that disputes can be settled peacefully to the rejection of all force. It has ancient precedents, took organised form in the peace movements of 1815 and 1816, and was named in 1901. It was shaped by Quakers, Tolstoy and Gandhi and criticised by those who held that war can prevent greater violence.
references: Andrew Fiala, The Routledge Handbook of Pacifism and Nonviolence (Routledge, 2018)
